Clone a website Open the project in your agent with browser access enabled. In Claude Code or Cursor, run: /clone-website https://example.com Replace the URL with the website you want to recreate. Observe — inspect desktop/mobile pages, extract real assets and fonts, and exercise alternate states. Build — implement editable components and working interactions; delegate independent sections when useful. Compare — review source and local pages at matched sizes/states, repair visible differences, and run the production check. Framer pages and animated sites have focused inspection guidance for responsive variants, media, sticky scenes, and scroll/time-driven motion. Direct HTTP or asset tools handle extraction where practical; browser comparisons establish appearance and behavior. Deliverables include route mappings, run instructions, comparison screenshots, and any remaining gaps. Get the code back in a modern format Learning — deconstruct how production sites achieve specific layouts, animations, and responsive behavior by working with real code Not Intended For Phishing or impersonation — this project must not be used for deceptive purposes, impersonation, or any activity that breaks the law. title: ItzCrazyKns/Vane
abstract: Vane 🔍 Vane is a privacy-focused AI answering engine that runs entirely on your own hardware. It combines knowledge from the vast internet with support for local LLMs (Ollama) and cloud providers (OpenAI, Claude, Groq), delivering accurate answers with cited sources while keeping your searches completely private. Want to know more about its architecture and how it works? You can read it here . ✨ Features 🤖 Support for all major AI providers - Use local LLMs through Ollama or connect to OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Groq, and more. Mix and match models based on your needs. ⚡ Smart search modes - Choose Speed Mode when you need quick answers, Balanced Mode for everyday searches, or Quality Mode for deep research. 🧭 Pick your sources - Search the web, discussions, or academic papers. More sources and integrations are in progress. 🧩 Widgets - Helpful UI cards that show up when relevant, like weather, calculations, stock prices, and other quick lookups. 🔍 Web search powered by SearxNG - Access multiple search engines while keeping your identity private. Support for Tavily and Exa coming soon for even better results. 📷 Image and video search - Find visual content alongside text results. Search isn't limited to just articles anymore. 📄 File uploads - Upload documents and ask questions about them. PDFs, text files, images - Vane understands them all. 🌐 Search specific domains - Limit your search to specific websites when you know where to look. Perfect for technical documentation or research papers. 💡 Smart suggestions - Get intelligent search suggestions as you type, helping you formulate better queries. 📚 Discover - Browse interesting articles and trending content throughout the day. Stay informed without even searching. 🕒 Search history - Every search is saved locally so you can revisit your discoveries anytime. Your research is never lost. ✨ More coming soon - We're actively developing new features based on community feedback. Join our Discord to help shape Vane's future! Sponsors Vane's development is powered by the generous support of our sponsors. Their contributions help keep this project free, open-source, and accessible to everyone. We'd like to thank the following partners for their generous support: Exa • The Perfect Web Search API for LLMs - web search, crawling, deep research, and answer APIs Installation There are mainly 2 ways of installing Vane - With Docker, Without Docker. Using Docker is highly recommended. Getting Started with Docker (Recommended) Vane can be easily run using Docker. Simply run the following command: docker run -d -p 3000:3000 -v vane-data:/home/vane/data --name vane itzcrazykns1337/vane:latest This will pull and start the Vane container with the bundled SearxNG search engine. Once running, open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3000 . You can then configure your settings (API keys, models, etc.) directly in the setup screen. Note : The image includes both Vane and SearxNG, so no additional setup is required. The -v flags create persistent volumes for your data and uploaded files. Using Vane with Your Own SearxNG Instance If you already have SearxNG running, you can use the slim version of Vane: docker run -d -p 3000:3000 -e SEARXNG_API_URL=http://your-searxng-url:8080 -v vane-data:/home/vane/data --name vane itzcrazykns1337/vane:slim-latest Important : Make sure your SearxNG instance has: JSON format enabled in the settings Wolfram Alpha search engine enabled Replace http://your-searxng-url:8080 with your actual SearxNG URL. Then configure your AI provider settings in the setup screen at http://localhost:3000 . Advanced Setup (Building from Source) If you prefer to build from source or need more control: Ensure Docker is installed and running on your system. Clone the Vane repository: git clone https://github.com/ItzCrazyKns/Vane.git After cloning, navigate to the directory containing the project files. Build and run using Docker: docker build -t vane . docker run -d -p 3000:3000 -v vane-data:/home/vane/data --name vane vane Access Vane at http://localhost:3000 and configure your settings in the setup screen. Note : After the containers are built, you can start Vane directly from Docker without having to open a terminal. Non-Docker Installation Install SearXNG and allow JSON format in the SearXNG settings. Make sure Wolfram Alpha search engine is also enabled. Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/ItzCrazyKns/Vane.git cd Vane Install dependencies: npm i Build the application: npm run build Start the application: npm run start Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3000 to complete the setup and configure your settings (API keys, models, SearxNG URL, etc.) in the setup screen. Note : Using Docker is recommended as it simplifies the setup process, especially for managing environment variables and dependencies. See the installation documentation for more information like updating, etc. Troubleshooting Local OpenAI-API-Compliant Servers If Vane tells you that you haven't configured any chat model providers, ensure that: Your server is running on 0.0.0.0 (not 127.0.0.1 ) and on the same port you put in the API URL. You have specified the correct model name loaded by your local LLM server. You have specified the correct API key, or if one is not defined, you have put something in the API key field and not left it empty. Ollama Connection Errors If you're encountering an Ollama connection error, it is likely due to the backend being unable to connect to Ollama's API. To fix this issue you can: Check your Ollama API URL: Ensure that the API URL is correctly set in the settings menu. Update API URL Based on OS: Windows: Use http://host.docker.internal:11434 Mac: Use http://host.docker.internal:11434 Linux: Use http://<private_ip_of_host>:11434 Adjust the port number if you're using a different one. Linux Users - Expose Ollama to Network: Inside /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service , you need to add Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434" . (Change the port number if you are using a different one.) Then reload the systemd manager configuration with systemctl daemon-reload , and restart Ollama by systemctl restart ollama . For more information see Ollama docs Ensure that the port (default is 11434) is not blocked by your firewall. Lemonade Connection Errors If you're encountering a Lemonade connection error, it is likely due to the backend being unable to connect to Lemonade's API. To fix this issue you can: Check your Lemonade API URL: Ensure that the API URL is correctly set in the settings menu. Update API URL Based on OS: Windows: Use http://host.docker.internal:8000 Mac: Use http://host.docker.internal:8000 Linux: Use http://<private_ip_of_host>:8000 Adjust the port number if you're using a different one. Ensure Lemonade Server is Running: Make sure your Lemonade server is running and accessible on the configured port (default is 8000). Verify that Lemonade is configured to accept connections from all interfaces ( 0.0.0.0 ), not just localhost ( 127.0.0.1 ). Ensure that the port (default is 8000) is not blocked by your firewall. Using as a Search Engine If you wish to use Vane as an alternative to traditional search engines like Google or Bing, or if you want to add a shortcut for quick access from your browser's search bar, follow these steps: Open your browser's settings. Navigate to the 'Search Engines' section. Add a new site search with the following URL: http://localhost:3000/?q=%s . Replace localhost with your IP address or domain name, and 3000 with the port number if Vane is not hosted locally. Click the add button. Now, you can use Vane directly from your browser's search bar. Using Vane's API Vane also provides an API for developers looking to integrate its powerful search engine into their own applications. You can run searches, use multiple models and get answers to your queries. For more details, check out the full documentation here .

title: cjpais/Handy
abstract: Handy A free, open source, and extensible speech-to-text application that works completely offline. Handy is a cross-platform desktop application that provides simple, privacy-focused speech transcription. Press a shortcut, speak, and have your words appear in any text field. This happens on your own computer without sending any information to the cloud. Why Handy? Handy was created to fill the gap for a truly open source, extensible speech-to-text tool. As stated on handy.computer : Free : Accessibility tooling belongs in everyone's hands, not behind a paywall Open Source : Together we can build further. Extend Handy for yourself and contribute to something bigger Private : Your voice stays on your computer. Get transcriptions without sending audio to the cloud Simple : One tool, one job. Transcribe what you say and put it into a text box How It Works Press a configurable keyboard shortcut: hold it to record and release to stop, or tap it to toggle recording on and off (Hold-only and Toggle-only modes are also available) Speak your words while the shortcut is active Release and Handy processes your speech using Whisper Get your transcribed text pasted directly into whatever app you're using The process is entirely local: Silence is filtered using VAD (Voice Activity Detection) with Silero Transcription uses your choice of models: Whisper models (Small/Medium/Turbo/Large) with GPU acceleration when available Parakeet V3 - CPU-optimized model with excellent performance and automatic language detection Works on Windows, macOS, and Linux Quick Start Installation Download the latest release from the releases page or the website macOS : Also available via Homebrew cask : brew install --cask handy Windows : Also available via winget : winget install cjpais.Handy Note: The Homebrew cask and winget package are not maintained by the Handy developers. Debian/Ubuntu : Install the downloaded .deb with APT so required dependencies are installed automatically: sudo apt install ./Handy_ * .deb Do not use dpkg -i unless the dependencies are already installed. If you already used it, run sudo apt --fix-broken install . Install the application Launch Handy and grant necessary system permissions (microphone, accessibility) Configure your preferred keyboard shortcuts in Settings Start transcribing! Development Setup For detailed build instructions including platform-specific requirements, see BUILD.md . Sponsors We're grateful for the support of our sponsors who help make Handy possible: Integrations Control Handy from Raycast — start/stop recording, browse transcript history, manage dictionary, switch models and languages. Source · by @mattiacolombomc Debug Mode Handy includes an advanced debug mode for development and troubleshooting. Access it by pressing: macOS : Cmd+Shift+D Windows/Linux : Ctrl+Shift+D CLI Parameters Handy supports command-line flags for controlling a running instance and customizing startup behavior. These work on all platforms (macOS, Windows, Linux). Largely this is a beta feature. Remote control flags (sent to an already-running instance via the single-instance plugin): handy --toggle-transcription # Toggle recording on/off handy --toggle-post-process # Toggle recording with post-processing on/off handy --cancel # Cancel the current operation Startup flags: handy --start-hidden # Start without showing the main window handy --no-tray # Start without the system tray icon handy --debug # Enable debug mode with verbose logging handy --help # Show all available flags Flags can be combined for autostart scenarios: handy --start-hidden --no-tray macOS tip: When Handy is installed as an app bundle, invoke the binary directly: /Applications/Handy.app/Contents/MacOS/Handy --toggle-transcription Known Issues & Current Limitations This project is actively being developed and has some known issues . We believe in transparency about the current state: Bluetooth Headset Microphones (macOS) Using a Bluetooth headset microphone on macOS may temporarily reduce playback quality or volume while recording because Bluetooth switches to bidirectional audio. Keep your headphones as the output device and select your Mac's built-in or an external microphone in Handy to avoid this. fn and Globe Key Shortcuts (macOS) Shortcuts that include the fn (Globe) key only work on Apple keyboards — your Mac's built-in keyboard or an Apple external keyboard. They will never trigger on a third-party keyboard, even while it is connected to the same Mac. This is a hardware limitation rather than a Handy bug. fn is not part of the standard USB HID keyboard specification: Apple reports it through a vendor-specific usage that macOS honors only from Apple devices, while third-party keyboards handle their Fn key entirely in firmware and send nothing to the computer. There is no event for Handy to listen for. If you switch between a MacBook keyboard and an external one, pick a shortcut built from standard modifiers ( ctrl , option , shift , command ) or a regular key instead. Linux Notes Text Input Tools: For reliable text input on Linux, install the appropriate tool for your display server: Display Server Recommended Tool Install Command X11 xdotool sudo apt install xdotool Wayland wtype sudo apt install wtype Both dotool sudo apt install dotool (requires input group) X11 : Install xdotool for both direct typing and clipboard paste shortcuts Ubuntu 26.04 : Has Wayland display server by default. wtype does not work, you need to install ydotool and configure systemd as described here . Wayland : Install wtype (preferred) or dotool for text input to work correctly dotool setup : Requires adding your user to the input group: sudo usermod -aG input $USER (then log out and back in) Without these tools, Handy falls back to enigo which may have limited compatibility, especially on Wayland. Wayland Support (Linux): Limited support for Wayland display server Requires wtype or dotool for text input to work correctly (see Linux Notes below for installation) Other Notes: Runtime library dependency ( libgtk-layer-shell.so.0 ) : Handy links gtk-layer-shell on Linux. If startup fails with error while loading shared libraries: libgtk-layer-shell.so.0 , install the runtime package for your distro: Distro Package to install Example command Ubuntu/Debian libgtk-layer-shell0 sudo apt install libgtk-layer-shell0 Fedora/RHEL gtk-layer-shell sudo dnf install gtk-layer-shell Arch Linux gtk-layer-shell sudo pacman -S gtk-layer-shell For building from source on Ubuntu/Debian, you may also need libgtk-layer-shell-dev . The recording overlay is disabled by default on Linux ( Overlay Position: None ) because certain compositors treat it as the active window. When the overlay is visible it can steal focus, which prevents Handy from pasting back into the application that triggered transcription. If you enable the overlay anyway, be aware that clipboard-based pasting might fail or end up in the wrong window. Handy disables the WebKit DMA-BUF renderer by default on Linux, but preserves explicit WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER values. For rendering workarounds, see Troubleshooting → Linux Startup Crashes or Instability . If Handy fails to start reliably on Linux, see Troubleshooting → Linux Startup Crashes or Instability . Global keyboard shortcuts (Wayland): On Wayland, system-level shortcuts must be configured through your desktop environment or window manager. agent-browser Browser automation CLI for AI agents. Fast native Rust CLI. Installation Global Installation (recommended) Installs the native Rust binary: npm install -g agent-browser
agent-browser install # Download Chrome from Chrome for Testing (first time only) Project Installation (local dependency) For projects that want to pin the version in package.json : npm install agent-browser
agent-browser install Then use via package.json scripts or by invoking agent-browser directly. Homebrew (macOS) brew install agent-browser
agent-browser install # Download Chrome from Chrome for Testing (first time only) Cargo (Rust) cargo install agent-browser
agent-browser install # Download Chrome from Chrome for Testing (first time only) From Source Requires Node.js 24+, pnpm 11+, and Rust. git clone https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-browser cd agent-browser
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm build:native # Requires Rust (https://rustup.rs) pnpm link --global # Makes agent-browser available globally agent-browser install Linux Dependencies On Linux, install system dependencies: agent-browser install --with-deps This exits nonzero if the package manager cannot install every required browser library. When run as root, this command calls the detected package manager directly. For non-root users, it uses sudo . If you are not root and sudo is unavailable, it reports that root privileges or sudo are required. Updating Upgrade to the latest version: agent-browser upgrade Detects your installation method (npm, Homebrew, or Cargo) and runs the appropriate update command automatically. Requirements Chrome - Run agent-browser install to download Chrome from Chrome for Testing (Google's official automation channel). Existing Chrome, Brave, Playwright, and Puppeteer installations are detected automatically. No Playwright or Node.js required for the daemon. macOS browser installation - On macOS versions below 13, agent-browser install stops before downloading Chrome for Testing and prints instructions to update macOS or install Chrome manually. Use Software Update if your Mac supports macOS 13 or later, or install Chrome manually from Google's Chrome download page . This check applies when you run agent-browser install ; the package installation commands above remain unchanged. If sw_vers -productVersion is unavailable, exits with an error, returns no version, or returns a malformed version, agent-browser install reports a detection error and stops before making a network request. Node.js 24+ and pnpm 11+ - Only needed when building from source. Rust - Only needed when building from source (see From Source above). Quick Start agent-browser open example.com
agent-browser snapshot # Get accessibility tree with refs agent-browser click @e2 # Click by ref from snapshot agent-browser fill @e3 " test@example.com " # Fill by ref agent-browser get text @e1 # Get text by ref agent-browser screenshot page.png
agent-browser close Clicks fail early when another element covers the target's click point, for example a consent banner or modal. Dismiss or interact with the reported covering element, then take a fresh snapshot before retrying the original ref. Click and dblclick fail, instead of reporting success, when the element is hidden, disabled, or outside the viewport. click --new-tab opens the link's URL directly, so these checks do not apply to it. Headless Chromium screenshots hide native scrollbars for consistent image output. Pass --hide-scrollbars false when launching to keep native scrollbars visible. Traditional Selectors (also supported) agent-browser click " #submit " agent-browser fill " #email " " test@example.com " agent-browser find role button click --name " Submit " Commands Core Commands agent-browser open # Launch browser (no navigation); stays on about:blank agent-browser open < url > # Launch + navigate to URL (aliases: goto, navigate) agent-browser read [url] # Fetch agent-readable text, or read rendered active-tab DOM agent-browser click < sel > # Click element (--new-tab to open in new tab) agent-browser dblclick < sel > # Double-click element agent-browser focus < sel > # Focus element agent-browser type < sel > < text > # Type into element agent-browser fill < sel > < text > # Clear and fill agent-browser press < key > # Press key (Enter, Tab, Control+a) (alias: key) agent-browser keyboard type < text > # Type with real keystrokes (no selector, current focus) agent-browser keyboard inserttext < text > # Insert text without key events (no selector) agent-browser keydown < key > # Hold key down agent-browser keyup < key > # Release key agent-browser hover < sel > # Hover element agent-browser select <sel> < val > # Select dropdown by value or visible label agent-browser check < sel > # Check checkbox agent-browser uncheck < sel > # Uncheck checkbox agent-browser scroll < dir > [px] # Scroll (up/down/left/right, --selector <sel>) agent-browser scrollintoview < sel > # Scroll element into view (alias: scrollinto) agent-browser drag < src > < tgt > # Drag and drop agent-browser upload < sel > < files > # Upload files agent-browser screenshot [path] # Take screenshot (--full for full page, saves to a temporary directory if no path) agent-browser screenshot --annotate # Annotated screenshot with numbered element labels agent-browser screenshot --if-changed # Recommended: skip unchanged images to save tokens agent-browser screenshot --threshold 0.01 # Ignore changes affecting at most 1% of pixels agent-browser screenshot --screenshot-dir ./shots # Save to custom directory agent-browser screenshot --screenshot-format jpeg --screenshot-quality 80
agent-browser pdf < path > # Save as PDF agent-browser snapshot # Accessibility tree with refs (best for AI) agent-browser eval < js > # Run JavaScript (-b for base64, --stdin for piped input) agent-browser connect < port > # Connect to browser via CDP agent-browser stream enable [--port < port > ] # Start runtime WebSocket streaming agent-browser webmcp list # List experimental page tools agent-browser webmcp invoke < tool > --params @input.json
agent-browser stream status # Show runtime streaming state and bound port agent-browser stream disable # Stop runtime WebSocket streaming agent-browser close # Close browser (aliases: quit, exit) agent-browser close --all # Close all active sessions agent-browser chat " <instruction> " # AI chat: natural language browser control (single-shot) agent-browser chat # AI chat: interactive REPL mode When the top-level Chrome/CDP eval result is a value JSON cannot represent, plain output prints its exact JavaScript token, including NaN , Infinity , -Infinity , -0 , BigInt literals, and undefined . With --json , data.result stays null and sibling data.unserializable contains the token. MCP text prints the token, and structured responses expose it at structuredContent.response.data.unserializable . WebMCP (experimental) WebMCP is enabled by default in agent-browser-managed Chrome. Use --no-webmcp to disable the launch features and proactive context. Browser responses automatically announce WebMCP tools on first discovery and when the catalog changes. Summaries contain only names, brief descriptions, origins, and frame IDs. Choose a relevant tool, then fetch its full schema with agent-browser webmcp list <tool> --frame <frame-id> --json before invoking it. Schemas and annotations are never included proactively. Unchanged catalogs and pages without tools add no context. JSON exposes updates as data.webmcp ; CLI and MCP text use the same summaries. An omitted field means no update. A one-time status: "ready" update with tools: [] clears previously advertised tools; status: "unavailable" invalidates them when observation fails. Every emitted summary replaces earlier availability, including schema-only changes. After conversation compaction or joining an existing browser session, use webmcp list to recover context.

title: leepokai/Codync
abstract:
Codync The open-source Grok Bot alternative. Bring your own agent and subscription — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and 40+ more — as teammates you can message from your phone. Website · Docs · Compare · Launch film · X @trycodync Free, open source, no paid tier. A ⭐ is how others find it; a ☕ keeps it going. macOS: Apple Silicon + Intel (DMG) · Windows: x64 installer · Linux: AppImage · All downloads Warning Official account: @trycodync is my only official account. Beware of impersonators and scams. Codync turns the coding agents on your computer — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi, OpenCode, Grok Build, Gemini, Copilot, Hermes Agent and ~40 more — into persistent bots you delegate to from your iPhone, Mac, Windows PC, Linux desktop or any terminal, the way you'd message a colleague. Pick who, say what, put the phone away. You get a notification when a bot finishes or needs your approval. Why bots? On a phone, "find the right working session, then pick an environment" is too slow. With bots you already know who to hand the intent to: open the chat, type, done. Why Codync Free and open source. No subscription, no paid tier, Apache 2.0 licensed. Bring your own subscription. Bots run on the Claude, ChatGPT or other plan your agents are already signed in with, on your own computer. Codync never calls a provider's API with your login. Agent-agnostic: bring any coding agent. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, Grok Build and ~40 more — everything in the ACP registry . Installed agents are found automatically, the rest are fetched on first use, and every bot picks its own. Mix them freely: a Claude bot can ask a Codex bot for a review. Many bots, one team. Run as many bots as you like side by side, each with its own agent, project folder and approvals, all working at once. Put several in a group chat and they answer in turn, like a team channel; @name picks who replies. Reply to any message, yours or a bot's, right in the chat. Built in Rust. codync-host is one small, fast Rust binary for macOS, Windows and Linux (static on Linux, runs on any distro) that drives every agent, keeps the transcripts and serves every client. One app per kind of device. Native SwiftUI on the iPhone, one desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux (Electron), and a terminal UI for SSH. A Grok Bot, Muse and Dots alternative. Persistent named bots, group chats, quote replies, bots asking each other for help, approval cards, per-bot memory, remote screen, voice calls and "needs you / done" notifications — the same features, without being tied to one model or one subscription. Reach your computer from anywhere, free. The hosted Cloudflare relay is included at no cost: no Tailscale, no VPN, no port forwarding. Traffic is end-to-end encrypted between your phone and your computer, so the relay only forwards ciphertext. Same Wi-Fi or Tailscale? The phone connects directly instead. Every computer, one app. Sign in and your iPhone lists every computer on your account (Mac, Windows PC, Linux desktop, server or cloud VM); open Computers and tap Ask for access , confirm a 6-digit code on that computer, and its bots show up next to the others. A new bot can live on any of them, and the desktop app on Mac, Windows and Linux reaches your SSH machines too. Each computer approves each device itself, so an account alone never unlocks a computer. Remote screen. See and control your computer from the iPhone over WebRTC (hardware H.264), and let bots use the screen themselves through the built-in computer tool. Voice calls. Talk to a bot hands-free from the iPhone and hear its replies read aloud. Private push. Notification text is sealed to your phone's key, so the push relay never sees what your bots said. Platforms Platform App Highlights 📱 iPhone Native SwiftUI Chat with bots, approvals, push notifications, Live Activity, widgets, remote screen, voice calls 💻 macOS Desktop app (Electron), menu bar + window Runs the host, chat window, usage in the menu bar, iPhone pairing 🪟 Windows Desktop app (Electron), tray + window Runs the host, chat window, iPhone pairing (no remote screen yet) 🐧 Linux Desktop app (Electron), tray + window Chat window, iPhone pairing; the host runs on desktops and headless servers ⌨️ Terminal codync-host tui Message your bots from any terminal, over SSH too The host ( codync-host , Rust) runs on macOS, Windows and Linux; every client talks to it, so all your bots and chats are the same everywhere. Looking for the former native Mac app (SwiftUI + AppKit)? Version 2.7.0 moved Mac and
Linux to one Electron desktop app. The native implementation is preserved in Git history at 1055636 ; see the archived AppKit chat implementation notes . How it works Remote Apple client ⇄ encrypted channel (direct or Cloudflare cloud/) ⇄ codync-host ⇄ ACP agent
Local / SSH client  ⇄ loopback HTTP + SSE                             ⇄ codync-host
Host notifications → APNs worker (relay/) → iPhone Bots have a name, a character avatar, standing instructions, an agent backend, a project folder and a permission policy. Each bot has one persistent chat , where you can reply to any message; the agent sessions underneath are an implementation detail (resumed with session/load , restarted with New session ). Group chats hold several bots and you. Each message starts a short room turn: the bots you @-mention (or everyone) reply one at a time, each in its own session, and can react to each other, up to 3 rounds. See group chats and replies . Bots can ask each other for help. Tell one “ask Reviewer to check these changes.” The built-in team MCP server lets it discover your other visible bots and message one; the reply comes back to it as a new turn, and it answers you then. Requests appear in both chats; each recipient keeps its own agent, folder and approvals. Native subagents stay under the coding agent's control. See bot collaboration . The chat only shows what matters : your messages, each turn's final reply, approval cards and notices. Every tool call, diff, plan and thought is one tap away in Full conversation . While a bot works, its row shows what it's doing right now. Agents are detected automatically : the host hydrates PATH from your login shell (plus Homebrew, ~/.local/bin, nvm, bun, volta, asdf, mise, pnpm…), finds every harness you have installed, and prefers its native ACP mode. Anything else in the official ACP registry can be picked too — Codync fetches it on first use (npx, uvx or a checksummed binary). codync-host (Rust, macOS, Windows and Linux) runs on your computer. It speaks the Agent Client Protocol to each agent, keeps transcripts in SQLite, and serves the phone. Every change carries a global rev , so the phone reconnects with since: rev and never misses anything. Usage limits come from the agents installed on your computer. Claude uses claude -p /usage (a local command, no model call) plus Claude Code's status line, and the signed-in Codex CLI reports current account limits without a model call. oh-my-pi, Amp, Kiro, Kimi, Antigravity, OpenCode, Mistral Vibe and Junie are read from their own command, database or IDE file. Cursor asks cursor.com with the sign-in it saved locally. The phone, widgets and menu bar see the resulting limits. Push goes through a tiny relay that holds the APNs key. The phone trades its device token for an encrypted ticket; the host only ever holds tickets. UI patterns (roster, character avatars, approval cards, trace sheet, "needs you / done" notifications) follow Grok Bot. Install One line (macOS or Linux): curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leepokai/Codync/main/packaging/install.sh | sh On a Mac it installs the app (the host ships inside it); on Linux the host, plus the desktop app when a display is present. Add sh -s -- --host-only for servers and headless Macs. Re-run it to upgrade. Mac — download codync-macos.

title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
abstract:
One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?” Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward: Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised) Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.) Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating) Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.: I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test. To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR ), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite. Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs , etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required. One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance. With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results. Results I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.) The exception was Angular, which failed to create a measurable app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead for some metrics. (This is explained below.) Cost Cost per run, in US dollars Framework Cost ($) Hono+htmx $2.67 (2.23–3.19) −0.44 +0.52 Astro $2.76 (2.16–3.63) −0.60 +0.87 Nuxt $2.82 (2.39–4.25) −0.43 +1.43 Vanilla $2.98 (2.24–3.37) −0.74 +0.39 Next.js $3.14 (2.58–4.13) −0.56 +0.99 Qwik $3.27 (2.35–3.80) −0.92 +0.53 TanStack Start $3.54 (3.11–3.96) −0.43 +0.42 SolidStart $3.79 (2.84–4.81) −0.95 +1.02 React Router $3.81 (2.82–3.97) −0.99 +0.16 SvelteKit $4.28 (3.59–4.65) −0.69 +0.37 Gracile+Lit $4.65 (3.92–5.07) −0.73 +0.42 Angular $4.97 (3.19–6.82) −1.78 +1.85 0 2 4 6 8 Median of 5 runs. Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Cost ($), low to high Cost ($), high to low Show as table Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month. Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge. Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it’s too new to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from node_modules . For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below). I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one: Click to see AI tool usage Framework Installed Used by the agents? Angular Angular MCP and Angular agent skills MCP in 3/5 runs, skill tool in 4/5 runs, skill files in 2/5 Astro Astro MCP server MCP in 2/5 runs Gracile+Lit N/A N/A Hono+htmx Hono skills Skill tool in 5/5 runs Next.js next-devtools-mcp and next-dev-loop skill Skill files in 1/5 runs, AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs Nuxt Nuxt MCP N/A Qwik N/A N/A React Router React Router skill Skill tool in 5/5 runs, skill files in 5/5 runs SolidStart N/A N/A SvelteKit Svelte Claude Code plugin MCP in 5/5 runs TanStack Start N/A Skill files in 2/5 runs Vanilla N/A N/A For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the node_modules of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely). title: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Radio Signals from RAM (2024)
abstract:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security [Submitted on 3 Sep 2024] Title: RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM Authors: Mordechai Guri View a PDF of the paper titled RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM, by Mordechai Guri View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Air-gapped systems are physically separated from external networks, including the Internet. This isolation is achieved by keeping the air-gap computers disconnected from wired or wireless networks, preventing direct or remote communication with other devices or networks. Air-gap measures may be used in sensitive environments where security and isolation are critical to prevent private and confidential information leakage. In this paper, we present an attack allowing adversaries to leak information from air-gapped computers. We show that malware on a compromised computer can generate radio signals from memory buses (RAM). Using software-generated radio signals, malware can encode sensitive information such as files, images, keylogging, biometric information, and encryption keys. With software-defined radio (SDR) hardware, and a simple off-the-shelf antenna, an attacker can intercept transmitted raw radio signals from a distance. The signals can then be decoded and translated back into binary information. We discuss the design and implementation and present related work and evaluation results. This paper presents fast modification methods to leak data from air-gapped computers at 1000 bits per second. Finally, we propose countermeasures to mitigate this out-of-band air-gap threat. title: AI agent swarms in Minecraft fail to build civilization, drown in bureaucracy
abstract:
(Image credit: ycombinator ) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Subscribe to our newsletter AI researchers at ycombinator and Olam Labs recently tested AI agent swarms in gaming scenarios. Minecraft and its various game modes were the sandboxes where 100s of agents were unleashed to work together or as adversaries. The idea seems to be that the in-game collaborations and conflicts would provide insight into real-world headline-grabbing cases with AI agents involved. This study might help us see what happened, good and bad, in recent AI swarm cases, and thus developers of this technology can improve it. The blog mentions two contrasting cases, which were the thousand-agent swarms that “recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems,” and the “extremely dangerous” OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. This research is built on prior work and frameworks, specifically repos like Mindcraft and scripting tools in Mineflayer. Multi-agent dynamics in Minecraft The first AI swarm testing plan was a simple collaborative one. During this test phase, the researchers tasked 50 agents with building a thriving civilization in three hours. It seems to have tested 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents here, but not any Claude agents . Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: Probably the most interesting insight from this ‘Civ50’ test was that the 50-strong colony never really thrived. After the first night saw zombies take out a large number of agents (but with little penalty) it was noted that “many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.” From then on, the colonists cautiously survived, and there was a tendency toward bureaucracy. As an example, “four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block.” The researchers say this AI agent swarm behavior “felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents.” (Image credit: ycombinator ) Next up, the researchers decided to put AI agent swarms into conflict. First they tested them in Bed Wars, which is a kind of team PvP capture the base, while defending yours game mode. The setup was 10 GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents. “GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies,” noted the researchers. Claude was more defensive. It was also interesting to observe contrasts in how the teams handled problems. “A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible.” Finally, the agents were tested in Mindustry, a kind of light RTS combat game with tower defense mode in Minecraft. “The GPTs won 6-1 against the Claudes in the 7 games,” which was a great result for the OpenAI-created agents. Researchers concluded that GPTs acted more like a hive, while Claudes had a single leader but a democratic-style decision process. In Mindustry, the former was the foundation for a more consistently winning strategy. These swarms are open sourced so you can run your own, if you are interested in tweaking and testing. The source blog post ends with some open questions that you can check hands-on, offering some directions for investigative probing. For example, it is suggested that comparing different mixes of models and varying sizes of agent swarms in Minecraft might raise worthwhile conclusions. Previously: We got Claude Code playing Factorio , Towards beating Factorio autonomously , and Faketorio: an agent testbed I got GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with low thinking level, to complete a peaceful (i.e. no biters) Factorio run in 13.5 hours of game time: A timelapse of the full run is available on YouTube . Similar to my previous post , this run used a game manager to allow Sol/Codex to interact with the game via a small library (though in this run it was Python rather than Bash). The library allows the model to play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions that human players face when using the GUI (e.g. reach of the player, fog of war). Observing the run was fascinating: Sol exceeded my expectations in some areas while also showing clear weaknesses in others. I have the entire run recorded and am working on a commentary video, but in the meantime here’s a small timelapsed segment showing some parts of the factory: Besides the screencast, my run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. Here’s a chart of total resource production, annotated with science research milestones: I had planned to terminate the run after blue science research, but Sol’s surprising effectiveness convinced me to keep it going. Unfortunately, the scaling issues I thought would occur in the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol’s relative progress significantly. The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory. Still, I was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5 which suffered from the model’s failures to use transport belts at all. I’m optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. In many ways playing Factorio is analogous to programming but with the benefit of being much more legible to casual observers, making it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors. I look forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs. Stay tuned!

title: Copyright Office is restoring copyright to something you have to work to get
abstract:
Today's links Formalities : When it comes to AI, the Copyright Office is restoring copyright to its proper status, as something you have to work to get. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : GWB x martial law; Li'l Sparky; Dueling Starbuckses; Microsoft buys Skype (does fuckery); Bieber v SOPA; SOPA is the worst; Snowden x rule of law; "Laserwriter II"; Russia v DST; Class war funnies; Minnesota's miracle; Icelandic women v sexism; Image analogies; Aussie DMCA ratfucked; "Authorised Domain"; Sales tax is regressive; Prince Charles's secret veto; Wells Fargo blackballed workers for refusing to crime; Poe read by Vincent Price and Basil Rathbone; Put it back!; The internet was made for privacy. Upcoming appearances : Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Formalities ( permalink ) It's not often that I find myself on the same side as the US Copyright Office. In fact, I think this is the first time in 25 years that I've found myself cheering on the office's official actions as good for art and good for free expression, taking the side of creative workers over our bosses. The source of our miraculous accord: the US Copyright Office's position on AI. The CO has taken the (entirely correct) position that copyright law exists to incentivize human acts of creative expression, which means that only works of human authorship are eligible for copyright. This isn't a controversial position within legal circles. But for media executives, this is shocking; absurd, even. This gap between the industrial and the legal understanding of copyright comes from a fundamental difference over the evocatively named legal doctrine of "sweat of the brow." "Sweat of the brow" is fundamental to a correct legal understanding of copyright. Copyright rewards and protects creativity but it does not protect hard work . You can labor for ten years over a phone book listing the numbers of every person in a town and (as a collection of uncopyrightable facts) it will receive no protection at all . Zero. Zilch. Anyone can copy and sell that phone book: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feist_Publications,_Inc._v._Rural_Telephone_Service_Co. Copyright law doesn't care if you slaved over that collection of facts, if you missed sleep and your kids' little league games to realize your grand vision. Copyright law doesn't care if you plowed every cent into it, remortgaging your home and cashing in your (already resentful) kids' college funds. But: if you dash off a haiku in ten seconds while sitting on the toilet, shove it into your pocket and forget about it, and then your (still resentful) kids discover that crumpled haiku after your (highly suspicious) death, your kids will be able to claim a full 70 years' worth of copyright over that forgotten triviality (the term of copyright for works of human authorship is life plus 70 years). This is the uncontroversial and universally accepted legal understanding of copyright: all the copyright in the world for creative acts, no copyright at all for mere acts of labor. The "sweat of the brow" has nothing to do with a work's eligibility for copyright. But no media boss believes this. For media bosses, copyright is a pseudo-property† right, designed and operated to protect their bottom line. The point of copyright isn't to incentivize creativity , but rather investment . † Or not-so-pseudo There's obviously a relationship between creative acts and acts of investment, but it's possible to create without investment (see: your haiku) and it's possible to invest without creativity (see: your phone book). And once again, the creativity that copyright protects is human creativity. This is a lesson that David Slater learned the hard way. Slater is a professional wildlife photographer and amateur monkey-trainer who combined his interests by teaching Celebes crested macaque monkeys to take selfies. But when Slater published a monkey's selfie others copied and distributed the image without his permission, on the (entirely legally correct) basis that monkeys are not humans, and that means that works created by monkeys don't get a copyright. This was also the Copyright Office's position, and the position of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey_selfie_copyright_dispute This is the basis for the US Copyright Office's repeated decision to refuse to extend copyright to AI-generated works. An algorithm is even less human than a monkey, so if you can't get copyright over a monkey selfie, you definitely can't copyright your chatbot's slop. The US Copyright Office has successfully defended this position in multiple courts, triumphing over plaintiffs who were so persistent that they even got the Supreme Court to weigh in on the issue (the Supremes decided the case didn't warrant their attention): https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation AI slop isn't copyrightable, but there can be copyrightable elements in an AI-generated image. The most obvious element is the prompt. So long as your prompt contains some quantum of creativity (e.g. "Make me a beautiful flower whose loveliness is reminiscent of a newborn baby", but not "make me a beautiful flower"), that prompt is copyrightable. That means you can use copyright to challenge others' rights to present the same prompt to a chatbot. But while the prompt can be copyrighted, the image it gives rise to isn't . So you can spend a month iteratively refining your prompt, consuming all your town's water along with 200,000 gallons of diesel and that prompt will be yours for your life plus 70 years, but the image it generates is in the public domain, and anyone can copy it, sell it or give it away. There are other ways that copyright can find its way into AI-generated material. You can make creative edits to it: if you output a slop novel and rewrite various sentences (providing those rewrites involve some creativity and not just mechanical corrections or word substitutions), then the edited sentences become copyrighted works, even though all the rest of the text remains uncopyrightable. You can also get a "thin" copyright through selection. If you get your chatbot to output many images based on your prompt and choose your favorite, your selection can confer a tiny bit of copyright over that creative act of selection, but it will be harder to defend than even the other (attenuated and highly specific) forms of copyright. Now, perhaps you've spotted an administrative problem lurking in this turn of events. How can someone else know what part of a work is AI-generated (and thus in the public domain) and which parts are human-edited/contributed (and thus copyrighted)? Just as importantly, how can you prove which parts of your work are not AI-generated and thus eligible for copyright protection. This gets especially gnarly when you're dealing with complex media. In an animation, an AI might do the rigging and movement for a human-created sprite. The sprite is copyrightable, but its movements aren't. That would mean that I could remap your sprite's movements onto a different sprite without infringing your copyright. Or say the sprite and its movements are human created (and thus copyrighted), but the backgrounds are procedurally generated? I could take those backgrounds and put new animations overtop of them. The simplest, most reliable way to ensure the works you invest in are fully and entirely eligible for copyright is to just use humans for the whole project. Declare a "no-AI policy," and hire human artists to produce the works you hope to sell. Monitor their activity to ensure they're not using AI. Keep good records.

title: Altoids Project
abstract:
My 12-year-old son and I spent about two months on, what we call, the Altoids project. Here is the final product ( video ): It all started when I took him to MIT Swapfest for the first time. We saw an assembled robot from a couple’s booth; later we learned that it was from a kit . It was built by their daughter many years ago. After realizing I had come with my son, they gave us the robot for free. We also picked up a used ThinkPad laptop at a very reasonable price, which we used for the project. As any curious mind would, we disassembled the robot. Noticing that we were missing the control, we wanted to see which parts we could reuse. We took the 128x64 display off. But we couldn’t find the pinout for the display. We tried using AI, but it hallucinated so badly that it gave us a 20-pin pinout when the display only has 10 pins. After hours of searching around, we found the exact schematic posted on Arduino’s forum by a stranger on the Internet. God bless him. With the pinout, we finally made the display show something. We ran the Space Trash game from the U8g2 library . Let’s call this v1. I had just watched a YouTube video where someone built a tiny computer and fit everything inside an Altoids tin ( video ). Inspired by the YouTube video, we grabbed a random tin found in the house and moved the project to the workbench. To reduce the form factor, we switched to an Arduino Nano , and ordered LiPo batteries and PowerBoost for power supply. Everything needed to fit in the tin. My son did all the CAD and 3D printing. Here is what v2 looked like. The lid did not close. It felt like playing 3D chess to fit everything in. We ordered solderable breadboards to avoid the messy wires. It was looking promising. We also bought a real tin of Altoids from a grocery store, since the Altoids tin is actually a little taller than the one we were using earlier. This is what v3 looked like. The lid did not close, but we were getting closer. The display was connected to a tiny solderable breadboard. We wanted to remove it and connect the wires to the display directly. But we had a really hard time with desoldering. We accidentally pulled one copper pad off the display, making it unusable. We might be possible to salvage it, but we just ordered a new display from Adafruit instead. At this point, I wanted to avoid desoldering as much as possible. So we got those tiny hooks for testing the display ( video ). This is when we realized the new display does not default to SPI mode. We did not want to make more changes to the wiring, so we still had to desolder two jumpers. I suspected our soldering iron was heating unevenly. We ordered a new soldering iron and it made all the difference. With the new iron, we made rapid progress. We hot-glued the display onto the lid. Everything worked for the first time. This is what v4 looked like. The lid did close with some struggle. Two wires connecting the microcontroller and the display broke the next day. We did many hacks, one of which is to extend the wires by soldering two wires together. It did not work well, obviously. We got some ultra-fine (30 AWG) wires to replace them. At this point, my son did most of the desoldering and soldering work. He actually connected one wire incorrectly, so it did not work at first. It is a good debugging and learning experience. As a final touch, we got tiny 1x1-inch ziploc bags and put two actual Altoids in the tin. And here we have the final product, after five iterations. None of the components used in the first iteration survived.

title: Anthropic takes steps to block Claude from reverse-engineering video games
abstract:
Credit: J Studios / Getty Images According to reporting from Tom's Hardware , Anthropic's Claude AI has quietly started restricting the kinds of work it will do, including modding, decompiling, or reverse-engineering video game code. And though there has as yet been no official announcement about why , the reason is still pretty obvious. The video game community has been in the news a lot lately, first because of the GTA6 leaks that went mega-viral and spurred Take-Two Interactive into getting subpoenas against both Microsoft and Discord in the hopes of finding the responsible parties, and next because the hacking and modding community discovered how much easier AI makes their job. SEE ALSO: Claude's new smart reports tell bosses when workers are 'off-topic' First, game decompilers went into overdrive, playing around with the source code of multiple different video games to, for example, put Nintendo's Mario inside the dark gothic world of Elden Ring , or import Spider-Man into the Batman: Arkham City game , seamlessly blending the mechanics of one character into the world of another. Next came the ports: World of Warcraft , Call of Duty, and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City made playable in a browser, without the original developers or copyright owners having any say in the matter. Mashable Light Speed Want more out-of-this world tech, space and science stories? Sign up for Mashable's weekly Light Speed newsletter. Use this instead By clicking Sign Me Up, you confirm you are 16+ and agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy . Thanks for signing up! You May Also Like These initial modifications and ports were already giving gaming companies nightmares, teasing a future without system gatekeeping, but things really got out of hand with the PlayStation 5 jailbreak , which resulted in everything from backward compatibility with older-gen PlayStation games to cross-platform play, with users figuring out how to run Xbox-exclusive titles like Halo 2 and acclaimed Nintendo titles like Zelda: Breath of the Wild on a jailbroken PS5. Given the potential number of lawsuits these jailbreaks could cause, and the astronomically high nature of the monetary damages, it's no surprise that AI companies are scrambling to shut down or severely restrict these pathways, but it's also deeply ironic. As Tom's Hardware reporter Bruno Ferreira notes , this sudden concern for copyright "highlights the irony of frontier AI companies that copied the world's information and art for their training sets and are now concerned with copyright infringement." There's also the ugly truth that, if one company makes a gesture toward respecting copyright law or basic ethics, the bad actors can find another LLM that won't (or hasn't yet) taken the same precautions, creating a kind of AI arms race driven by perverse incentives: the least ethical AI might be poised to become the most popular. title: Entity-Dependent Relation Learning for Knowledge Graph Completion
abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to predict missing relationships between pairs of entities. Recently, Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have been employed in KGC and demonstrated superior ability in embedding learning. Current methods, however, face two major dilemmas. One focuses on learning complex entity embedding while neglecting the importance of relation embedding learning. The other is that some KGC methods conduct relation embedding learning through a neural network. However, this learning procedure limits learning independence from neighboring entities. To address this issue, we propose a Relation Entity Graph Message Passing mechanism (REGMP) to model the learning of entity-dependent relation embedding. Firstly, REGMP constructs a novel relation entity graph, which transforms relation edges into nodes with new edges and directions. The re-constructed relation entity graph builds a direct linkage between entities and relations during embedding learning. Besides, to conduct the embedding learning on the relation entity graph, we propose a Relation Entity Graph Message-passing mechanism to exploit local and fine-grained information. Moreover, to ease the inevitable over-smoothing problem, we develop a reaction-diffusion message-passing network. Experimental results on three knowledge graph completion datasets, including WN18RR, FB15k-237, and Kinship demonstrate the superiority of REGMP.

title: HAIFIT: Structure-Consistent Fashion Image Translation With Multiscale Feature Modeling
abstract: In the realm of fashion design, sketches serve as a medium for expressing distinctive drawing styles and creative intent, capturing intricate details like stroke variations and texture nuances. The advent of sketch-to-image translation technology has notably aided designers. However, existing methods often compromise these sketch details during image generation, resulting in images that deviate from the intended structural and stylistic characteristics of the input sketch. This limitation hampers the ability to offer designers a precise preview of the final output. To overcome this challenge, we introduce HAIFIT, a novel approach that transforms sketches into high-fidelity, lifelike clothing images by integrating multiscale features and capturing multidirectional feature dependencies to encourage structurally consistent representations. In addition, we develop a diffusion-based variant, D-HAIFIT, to provide a complementary benchmark for evaluating structural consistency and generative fidelity. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations conducted on the HAIFashion dataset, our method demonstrates superior experimental performance compared with the existing approaches, generating clothing images with improved structural consistency and fine-grained detail preservation for practical fashion design workflows. Furthermore, HAIFIT achieves faster training and inference, contributing to improved computational efficiency and reduced design iteration time.

title: Wonder Town: Integrating Generative AI into a Bloom-Aligned Physics Learning Game
abstract: Physics education remains challenging for many secondary-school students because core concepts such as forces, motion, electricity, and magnetism are abstract, counterintuitive, and frequently associated with persistent misconceptions. Although educational games and generative AI have shown potential to support learning, most existing systems position AI in a single role—such as a chatbot tutor or narrative generator—rather than integrating it throughout the broader learning experience. As a result, opportunities for adaptive support, sustained engagement, and cognitively scaffolded learning within game-based environments remain limited. This paper presents Wonder Town, a web-based physics learning serious game that integrates generative AI across multiple stages of a learning process structured around Bloom’s Taxonomy, a framework that supports progression from lower-order to higher-order thinking skills. The system combines AI-generated narrative styles, a diegetic AI mascot named Jules, reflective conversational feedback, and five hand-coded interactive physics simulations covering topics including motion, forces, friction, electricity, and magnetism. Wonder Town was developed iteratively and evaluated with secondary-school students and physics teachers through a mixed-methods design process. The paper contributes a Bloom-aligned multi-touchpoint design pattern for integrating generative AI into educational games. It also provides early evidence that embedding AI within a narrative-driven and cognitively scaffolded learning experience can support engaging, personalised, and educationally meaningful gameplay.

title: Large Language Models for DDoS Attack Detection: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks has posed significant threats to modern network infrastructure, overwhelming critical services and causing substantial operational disruptions. While traditional detection methods, including rule-based systems, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) approaches, have demonstrated limited effectiveness against increasingly sophisticated and evolving attack patterns, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing DDoS detection capabilities. This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of LLM-based DDoS attack detection research conducted between 2021 and 2026, following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMAs) guidelines. A comprehensive search across four major academic databases, namely IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, and Science Direct, yielded 891 articles, of which 25 studies met the eligibility criteria after rigorous screening. Five research questions (RQs) were formulated to examine: 1) the LLM architectures and models employed; 2) the datasets and evaluation metrics adopted; 3) the network environments and application scenarios targeted; 4) the computational efficiency and real-time performance characteristics; and 5) the main limitations and research gaps. The findings reveal that bidirectional encoder representations from Transformer (BERT)-based and generative pretrained transformer (GPT)-based architectures dominate the field, with fine-tuning being the most prevalent adaptation strategy. The CIC-DDoS2019 dataset is the most widely used benchmark, while Internet of Things (IoT) and software-defined networking (SDN) environments represent the primary application scenarios. Despite achieving high detection accuracy, existing approaches face critical challenges, including scalability constraints, limited real-time deployment capability, and insufficient generalization to unseen attack types. This review synthesizes current knowledge, identifies significant research gaps, and outlines future directions to guide the development of more robust and deployable LLM-based DDoS detection systems.

title: AGSM: Anchor-Guided Spatial–Semantic Modeling for Remote Sensing Image Captioning
abstract: Remote sensing image captioning (RSIC) aims to generate natural language descriptions for complex remote sensing imagery through effective cross-modal alignment between visual content and textual semantics. Due to densely distributed objects and complex spatial layouts, remote sensing scenes exhibit strong dependencies between local object details and global semantic context, posing significant challenges for discriminative visual representation learning. Existing methods struggle to capture such global–local dependencies and conduct targeted enhancement for key local regions, leading to fragmented global–local representations and limited semantic discriminability in generated captions. To address this issue, the Anchor-Guided Spatial-Semantic Modeling (AGSM) is proposed for RSIC. AGSM uses global–local semantic dependencies from CLIP-extracted CLS and patch tokens to guide feature enhancement and interaction. Specifically, a Visual Anchor Feature Diffusion (VAFD) module strengthens representative local features through anchor-based aggregation and diffusion. A Bi-Mamba Spatial Infusion (BMSI) module injects spatial dependencies into global semantic representations via bidirectional sequence modeling. Furthermore, a Spatially Gated FiLM-Mamba (SGFM) module, where FiLM denotes Feature-wise Linear Modulation, enables adaptive and cooperative global–local interaction through spatially adaptive modulation. The fused representations are finally decoded by a Mamba-based language decoder to generate accurate and coherent captions. Experimental results on four public benchmark datasets, including Sydney-Captions, UCM-Captions, RSICD, and NWPU-Captions, demonstrate the effectiveness and competitive performance of the proposed method.
